headline: Thunder is the sound of air exploding from heat—lightning's sonic signature
universal_truth: What we notice (thunder) often follows what causes it (lightning) by an observable delay
fun_facts: Lightning heats air to 30,000 Kelvin—five times hotter than the Sun's surface
You can estimate a storm's distance: count seconds between lightning and thunder, divide by 5 for miles
Thunder can be heard up to 15 miles away, but lightning can strike without audible thunder at greater distances
discussion_questions: What in your life is 'thunder' following 'lightning' you didn't notice?
Why do you think humans have always been awed by storms?
How does understanding thunder change the experience of a storm?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: Flash. Then rumble. Lightning and thunder—so familiar we rarely ask what's actually happening. Here's the truth: that deep rumble is the sound of air exploding. Lightning superheats air to five times hotter than the Sun's surface. That air has nowhere to go but outward. Fast.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Lightning is electricity—but thunder is sound. How does an electrical discharge create that massive, rolling boom? What's actually vibrating to make that noise?

options.text: Air superheated by lightning rapidly expands, creating a shockwave
options.response: Exactly. The sudden expansion of air at supersonic speed creates the boom we call thunder.

options.text: Lightning vibrates clouds, which produce the sound
options.response: Clouds don't make the sound—it's the air itself...

q1.title: Five Times Solar
q1.script: Lightning heats the air around it to about 30,000 Kelvin—five times hotter than the Sun's surface. This happens in a fraction of a second. The air can't handle it—it explodes outward in a shockwave. That explosion is thunder.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "Five Times Solar"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Count the Distance
q2.script: Light travels almost instantly, but sound moves at about one mile every 5 seconds. If you see lightning, count seconds until thunder. Five seconds means one mile away. Fifteen seconds, three miles. Simple physics becomes a safety tool.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: The Rolling Rumble
q3.script: Why does thunder roll instead of just crack? Lightning bolts are long—sometimes miles. Sound from different parts of the bolt reaches your ears at different times. The rolling effect is distance and reflection creating a chorus of arrivals.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Thunder reminds us that effects often follow causes after a delay. The consequences of our actions—good or bad—may rumble toward us long after the moment passed. Pay attention to the lightning, not just the thunder.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 40—forty days of learning! Tomorrow, we'll discover how rainbows form. Until then, next time you hear thunder, picture air exploding from heat you can't imagine. That's what you're hearing.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Cause and Effect - Lightning Before Thunder
growTrack.learning_objective: Notice the delay between causes and their effects
growTrack.activity: Think of a consequence you're experiencing now—good or bad. Trace it back to its 'lightning'—the action or decision that caused it. How long was the delay? This exercise builds awareness of delayed effects.
